description: In exactly three lines of dialogue, establish who the characters are, where they are, and what's happening — drilling the rapid scene-setting every story opening needs.
instructions: 1. Two players (or one person voicing both). 2. Line 1: player A establishes the relationship/who ('Grandpa, you promised you'd stop driving'). 3. Line 2: player B establishes the where ('and yet here we are, parked across two spaces at the funeral home'). 4. Line 3: player A establishes the what/conflict ('Mom is going to lose it when she sees this'). 5. Stop — the scene is set in three lines. 6. Repeat with new combinations until you can plant who/where/what fast and naturally. Apply to story openings: can you orient a listener in three sentences?
variations: Do it in two lines (harder); or open one of your real stories using only three orienting sentences.

name: Propp Function Cards
description: Draw cards from Vladimir Propp's 31 fairytale functions in order and improvise a folktale that hits each drawn beat, internalizing classic narrative grammar.
instructions: 1. Make a deck of cards, one per Propp function (e.g. Absentation — someone leaves; Interdiction — a warning is given; Violation — the warning is ignored; Villainy; Departure; Donor test; Receipt of a magical agent; Struggle; Victory; Return; Pursuit; Wedding/reward). 2. Shuffle a subset of 6-10 cards but keep them in Propp's ascending order. 3. Improvise a tale aloud that hits each function as it comes. 4. As a checklist drill, take a story you already tell and label which Propp functions it contains — and which classic beats it's missing. 5. Repeat with different function subsets.
setup: a set of Propp function cards (printable)
origin: Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (31 functions)
variations: Use Propp's 7 character roles (hero, villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, false hero) as casting cards for a story instead.

name: Data Story Arc (Big Idea Worksheet)
description: Turn a chart or dataset into a three-act narrative — setup, the tension of the insight, the call to action — boiling it down to one 'Big Idea' sentence first.
instructions: 1. Take a dataset or dashboard. 2. Write the BIG IDEA in a single sentence: what you want the audience to know and do, and what's at stake if they don't. 3. Build the arc: SETUP (the context everyone agrees on), TENSION (the surprising or worrying thing the data reveals), RESOLUTION (the recommended action). 4. Give the chart a 'takeaway title' that states the point, not the topic ('Churn doubled after the price change', not 'Monthly churn'). 5. Tell the three-act version aloud in under two minutes without reading numbers off the slide. 6. Drill on several datasets.
setup: a dataset or chart; pen and paper
origin: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, Storytelling with Data / Let's Practice!
variations: Dashboard-to-story drill: take a static dashboard and narrate the single most important story hiding in it.

name: Jump Tale
description: Tell a scary story engineered around a final 'jump' — voice dropping to a whisper, then a sudden shout or grab — drilling suspense control and a payoff that physically startles.
instructions: 1. Pick or build a short scary story with a single shock ending (the hand on the shoulder, the call coming from inside the house). 2. Pace the body of it SLOW: lower volume, lengthen pauses, lean in, use sensory detail (the crunch of leaves, the cold). 3. Hold eye contact during the longest pause to ratchet tension. 4. At the climax, drop nearly to a whisper, then deliver the final line as a sudden loud shout (and, with consent, a physical grab toward a listener) so everyone jumps. 5. Practice the whisper-to-shout transition until the timing reliably lands the startle. 6. Debrief on where suspense sagged.
origin: Campfire / oral ghost-story tradition (the jump tale)
variations: Slow-burn dread version with no jump (the horror is the implication); urban-legend 'this happened to a friend of a friend' framing.

name: Life Timeline (Stones and Flowers)
description: Draw your life as a timeline marking hard moments ('stones') and good ones ('flowers'), then mine the richest marks for stories — a personal-narrative finding tool from narrative therapy.
instructions: 1. Draw a horizontal line: birth on the left, today on the right. 2. Above the line, mark FLOWERS (moments of joy, pride, connection); below it, mark STONES (losses, failures, fears) — a word or symbol each, 10-20 total. 3. Circle the three marks that still carry a charge when you look at them. 4. For each, jot one sensory detail and the change it caused. 5. Develop one into a 3-minute told story this week; queue the rest. 6. Revisit the timeline every few months — new marks and new meaning appear.
variations: Theme timelines (love life, working life, friendships); chapter-titles version where you name each era of your life like book chapters.

name: Externalize the Antagonist
aliases: Name the Problem as a Character
description: Recast an internal struggle (anxiety, procrastination, a bad habit) as a named external character in your story, making a formless feeling into a vivid, tellable antagonist.
instructions: 1. Pick a personal struggle you'd like to tell a story about (self-doubt, anger, 'the slump'). 2. Externalize it: give it a name and a body — 'the Gremlin', 'Sergeant Should', 'the Fog' — and describe how it talks, moves, and tries to win. 3. Tell the story as a contest between you and this character: the moves it made, the counter-moves you made. 4. End on a specific moment you got the upper hand (a 'unique outcome'). 5. This turns vague emotional material into a concrete, often funny, narrative with a real antagonist and stakes.
variations: Unique-outcome log: each night write what you did, what it cost, and what it proves about you — a nightly story-seed habit.

name: String of Pearls
description: A group is given the first and last sentence of a story, then players fill in the missing middle sentences out of order, repeating the whole string each time so it builds into a coherent tale.
instructions: 1. With 6-8 players in a line: player 1 says a strong opening line; the player at the far end says an unrelated closing line. 2. Anyone may now step in and add ONE sentence anywhere between them that helps the two ends eventually connect. 3. After each new pearl is added, the whole line re-tells every sentence so far in order, first to last, so everyone hears the growing story. 4. Continue adding middle pearls until the leap from start to finish makes sense. 5. Debrief on which pearls did the most connective work. Solo/written version: write a first and last line, then fill the gap with stepping-stone sentences.
origin: Improv game String of Pearls (Michele Lowe play namesake)
variations: Ask the audience for the genre or just the first line; smaller pairs version filling a 4-sentence gap.

name: Cast of Thousands
description: Pick random numbers that map to pre-written lists of settings, heroes, villains, problems, and solutions, then tell a story that uses every element drawn — training fast integration of fixed constraints.
instructions: 1. Prepare five numbered lists in advance: SETTINGS, HEROES, VILLAINS, PROBLEMS, SOLUTIONS (10 entries each). 2. Without looking, pick a number for each list (or roll dice). 3. Read off your five elements — e.g. setting: a submarine; hero: a retired clown; villain: a polite accountant; problem: the coffee ran out; solution: a forgotten lullaby. 4. Immediately tell a 2-3 minute story that uses ALL five with a clear arc. 5. No swapping elements you dislike — the constraint is the training. 6. Re-draw and repeat.
setup: five pre-made numbered lists (or printable story-element tables)
variations: Use commercial story dice (Story Time Dice / Rory's Cubes) as the randomizer; add a 'required phrase' constraint.

name: Nanofiction Four-Card Build
description: Draw one card each for character, setting, problem, and resolution, then tell a complete short story weaving all four — drilling the minimum complete-story skeleton.
instructions: 1. Make (or use) four small decks: CHARACTERS, SETTINGS, PROBLEMS, RESOLUTIONS. 2. Draw one card from each. 3. Take 30 seconds, then tell a complete 60-90 second story that includes the character in the setting, facing the problem, reaching the resolution. 4. The discipline: the story must actually RESOLVE via the drawn resolution, not trail off. 5. In a group, each person draws a hand of several cards and competes to tell the best four-card story; others vote. 6. Reshuffle and repeat.
variations: Write the four categories on sticky notes from a brainstorm instead of using cards.

name: Multi-POV Same Event
description: Tell the same event several times in a row, each from a different character's point of view, training perspective control and revealing how POV changes a story's meaning.
instructions: 1. Pick one short event with at least three people present (a fender-bender, a surprise party gone wrong, a job interview). 2. Tell it first from character A's first-person POV — what they noticed, wanted, feared. 3. Retell the SAME events from character B's POV, then C's. 4. Keep the external facts consistent; only the lens changes. 5. Notice how sympathy and even the 'villain' shifts each time. 6. Application: find the moment in one of your true stories where the other person's POV would surprise your audience, and weave it in.
origin: Improv 'Point of View' / Rashomon narrative tradition
variations: Group version: assign each player a witness; they tell their POV in turn, then debate whose account to believe.

name: Punch-Word Marking
description: Mark the single most important word in each key sentence of a story and rehearse hitting only those, training emphasis that guides the listener's attention.
instructions: 1. Write out (or outline) a passage of your story. 2. In each sentence, underline the ONE word that carries the meaning — the 'punch word' (often a verb, a name, or a surprising noun). 3. Say the sentence stressing that word and flattening the rest; over-stressing everything is the same as stressing nothing. 4. Read the whole passage hitting only your marked words; record it. 5. On playback, check that a listener could follow the gist from the stressed words alone. 6. Re-mark anything that sounded monotone or wrongly emphasized.
variations: Contrast drill: deliberately stress the WRONG word in a sentence and hear how it changes or breaks the meaning.

name: Let the Audience Finish the Line
description: Build a moment so clearly that you can pause before the obvious next word and let listeners say it with you, training setup clarity and audience involvement.
instructions: 1. Find a beat in your story where the next word or outcome is highly predictable once you've set it up well ('I reached for the brake and hit the... '). 2. Set the moment up cleanly, then PAUSE on a rising, questioning inflection just before the predictable word, and make eye contact. 3. Hold the silence; let the audience supply the word (aloud or in their heads). 4. If they don't, your setup wasn't clear enough — tighten it. 5. Practice on a few setups; this is the engine of both comic timing and audience connection.
setup: a story with a setup-payoff beat
variations: Comic version: set up an expected word, pause, then deliver an unexpected one for a laugh (subverted anticipation).

name: Emotion-Mapped Read-Aloud
description: Take a written story (or picture book) and pre-mark its emotional highs and lows, then read it aloud matching voice, pace, and gesture to each marked beat — a delivery drill using ready-made text.
instructions: 1. Choose a short story or a dialogue-rich picture book. 2. Read it once silently, marking the emotional curve: where it's tense, tender, funny, scary, triumphant. 3. Plan a vocal/physical choice for each marked beat — slow and hushed for tension, bright and quick for joy, a droll voice for a sly character, a shrug acted out for 'he shrugged'. 4. Read it aloud fully committed to the map, big clean gestures. 5. Record and review; adjust any beat that read flat. 6. Repeat with new texts to widen your range using material you didn't have to write.
setup: a short story or picture book; optional recorder
variations: Read the same paragraph three times with three different dominant emotions; have a listener name each.

name: Object Autobiography
description: Tell the life story of an everyday object in first person — its making, its owners, what it has witnessed — training POV invention, voice, and finding narrative in the mundane.
instructions: 1. Pick any object (a park bench, a ten-dollar bill, your phone, a wedding ring). 2. Become it: speak in first person ('I was poured into a mold in a factory in Ohio...'). 3. Cover a small arc — its origin, the hands it passed through, the one moment it would never forget, where it is now. 4. Keep its 'voice' consistent (a weary coin sounds different from an excited new toy). 5. Tell it aloud in 2-3 minutes. 6. The drill builds the muscle of inhabiting a perspective not your own and finding story in objects.
origin: Classic composition/creative-writing exercise (autobiography of an object)
variations: Autobiography of a place (a kitchen, a crossroads); have a pair interview the object ('So, ring, how did you two meet?').

name: Moral-First Story Build
description: Start from a moral, proverb, or lesson and invent a fresh original story that delivers it — the Toastmasters storytelling drill, training intentional theme and payoff.
instructions: 1. Pick a moral or proverb ('slow and steady wins', 'pride before a fall', 'measure twice, cut once'). 2. Do NOT retell the famous fable; invent a brand-new story — modern, personal, or fantastical — whose events naturally demonstrate the lesson. 3. Build it so the moral is felt by the end without you stating it baldly. 4. Tell it in 3-5 minutes; ask listeners to guess the moral. 5. If they can't, your events didn't carry it — revise the plot, not the moral. 6. Repeat with new morals.
origin: Toastmasters Storytelling manual ('The Moral of the Story')
variations: Pull a fortune-cookie slip or a song lyric as the 'moral' to build around.

name: In Medias Res Opening
description: Rewrite a story's opening to drop the listener straight into the most charged moment, then loop back to fill in context — drilling hooks and non-linear structure.
instructions: 1. Take a story you currently tell chronologically. 2. Find its most gripping single moment (the crash, the confession, the door opening). 3. Start your telling THERE, in present-tense vivid detail, with no preamble: 'I'm hanging off the ladder by one hand and the dog is barking and...'. 4. Once you've hooked the listener, rewind: 'Okay — let me back up. Two hours earlier...' and fill in just enough context. 5. Return to and pass through the opening moment later. 6. Compare audience attention in the first 15 seconds versus your old chronological start.
origin: Classical narrative technique (in medias res), used across oral storytelling
variations: Flash-forward tease: open on a one-line glimpse of the ending, then tell the story toward it.

name: Epiphany Bridge Story
aliases: How I Came to Believe Story
description: Tell the story of the moment YOU came to believe something, so a listener feels the realization instead of being argued into it — a persuasion-through-story drill.
instructions: 1. Pick a belief or recommendation you want someone to adopt (a tool, an idea, a way of doing things). 2. Instead of listing reasons, tell the origin story of your own conversion: the BACKSTORY (what you wanted and why), the WALL you hit, the EPIPHANY (the moment it clicked), the new PLAN you tried, and the RESULT. 3. Use plain, emotional, jargon-free language — relive the realization, don't summarize it. 4. End at your result and let the listener draw the conclusion. 5. Tell it in under 2 minutes; test whether listeners feel persuaded rather than lectured.
variations: Use it to share why you love a hobby or place on a date, instead of reciting facts about it.

name: Recipe Origin Story
description: Tell the story behind a family or favorite recipe — who made it, the kitchen, the occasion — turning food into a warm personal narrative.
instructions: 1. Pick a dish that carries memory (grandmother's stew, the meal after a funeral, the first thing you cooked for someone). 2. Don't recite the recipe — tell its STORY: the person, the kitchen sounds and smells, the occasion, the small drama (the time it burned, the secret ingredient nobody admitted). 3. Anchor in sensory detail (the senses are vivid with food). 4. End on what the dish means to you now. 5. Tell it in 3-4 minutes. 6. The food gives the audience instant sensory access; practice using that.
variations: Tell the story while actually cooking or sharing the dish; do a 'taste this and I'll tell you why' framing at a gathering.

name: Tell Your Dream as a Story
description: Recount a real (or invented) dream as a coherent told story, imposing just enough structure on surreal material to keep a listener oriented — training shaping of chaotic content.
instructions: 1. On waking, jot a dream's images and feelings before they fade (keep a dream log). 2. Later, tell it as a story to a listener — but impose minimal order: a starting situation, one through-line to follow, and an ending beat (even if the dream had none, choose where to stop). 3. Keep the dream's strangeness but cut tangents that lose the listener. 4. Lean into the emotional logic ('it made no sense but I was terrified') rather than literal sense. 5. Debrief: where did the listener get lost? That's where dreams need the storyteller's shaping hand.
origin: Creative-writing dream-journal practice adapted to oral telling
variations: Invent a fake dream on the spot from three random images; tell a recurring dream and what you think it means.

name: Image Theatre Story (Dynamize the Tableau)
description: A group sculpts frozen body-images of a story's key moments, then 'dynamizes' them — bringing each tableau to life with one line or movement — to discover a narrative without words first.
instructions: 1. Pick a theme or situation (a conflict, a turning point). 2. Group members use their bodies to build a frozen image (tableau) capturing it — no talking, just shapes and relationships. 3. Build 3-5 tableaux representing the start, the crisis, and the resolution of a story — a wordless storyboard. 4. 'Dynamize' each: on a cue, every figure in the tableau makes one small movement or speaks one line of inner thought, bringing the still image alive. 5. Then narrate the story that connects the images aloud. 6. Debrief: the bodies often find truths words would have skipped. Pairs version: 'Complete the Image' — A strikes a pose, B adds a complementary pose, A clears and re-completes, building an evolving story.
origin: Augusto Boal, Theatre of the Oppressed (Image Theatre / Complete the Image)
variations: Sculpt a 'real' image of a problem and an 'ideal' image of its resolution, then improvise the transition story between them.

name: Seanchaí Formula Telling
description: Tell a tale from memory using rhythmic repeated 'runs' and formulaic phrases (the way Irish seanchaithe and Homeric bards did) to aid recall and give the telling musicality.
instructions: 1. Choose a story to tell from memory (a folktale or a long personal saga). 2. Build in formulaic devices: a recurring stock phrase for transitions ('they traveled the long day and the short day...'), a rhythmic 'run' you can recite for set pieces (a journey, a feast, a battle), and a repeated refrain at each turning point. 3. Learn the runs by heart as rhythmic units, not word-by-word. 4. Tell the story leaning on these formulas to carry you between remembered scenes — they buy you thinking time and please the ear. 5. Notice how repetition and rhythm both aid YOUR memory and pull listeners in. 6. Tell it twice; let the runs sharpen.
origin: Irish seanchaí oral tradition (and Homeric bardic formula)
variations: Add a sung or chanted refrain (ballad style); invent your own signature opening and closing formula to bookend every story you tell.

name: Five-Shot Photo Story
description: Plan or tell a story as five deliberate 'shots' — wide establishing, detail, portrait/face, action, and a closing image — borrowing photojournalism's shot list to build a complete visual narrative.
instructions: 1. Take a real event or outing you want to tell. 2. Choose five mental 'shots' that, together, tell it: (1) WIDE — establishes where we are; (2) DETAIL — a tight close-up of one telling object; (3) PORTRAIT — a face and what it shows; (4) ACTION — the key thing happening; (5) CLOSER — the image you end on. 3. Tell the story by walking through those five images in order, describing each vividly. 4. Notice you've covered context, character, detail, and emotion without a sprawling chronology. 5. Drill on several events; it trains selecting the few images that carry a whole experience.
origin: Photojournalism 'five shots' framework adapted to oral telling
variations: Actually shoot five photos on a walk, then tell the story they make; pass five random photos to someone to sequence and tell.

name: Future Headline Story
description: Write a headline about an accomplishment five years from now, hand it to a partner, and have them tell the story of how it happened — training vision-casting and reverse-engineered narrative.
instructions: 1. Write the headline you'd love to see about yourself (or your project) five years out: 'Local Teacher Opens Free Coding School for 500 Kids'. 2. Hand the headline to a partner. 3. The partner improvises the STORY behind it: the struggle, the turning point, how it came to be — as if reporting it. 4. Then you tell your own version and compare. 5. Debrief on which details made the future feel real. 6. The drill builds the skill of narrating a vision as a concrete story rather than a vague hope.
variations: Group gallery: post everyone's headlines on a wall; pick one and tell its backstory cold.

name: Eulogy / Obituary for a Stranger
description: Compose and deliver a short eulogy or obituary — for yourself, a stranger from a photo, or a fictional person — distilling a whole life into a few defining, telling moments.
instructions: 1. Pick a subject: your own future self, a stranger from an old photo, or an invented character. 2. Resist listing facts; instead choose 2-3 small specific moments or habits that reveal who they were ('he always over-tipped diner waitresses and never said why'). 3. Find the through-line — the one thing this life was 'about'. 4. Write a 60-90 second eulogy built from those moments, ending on the line you'd want remembered. 5. Deliver it aloud. 6. The constraint of a whole life in 90 seconds is brutal, excellent training in selection and meaning.
origin: Reflective-writing 'write your own obituary' exercise; toast/eulogy craft
variations: Toast version: deliver a 60-second toast for a friend built from three specific moments, not generic praise.
